_comment: The Orthodox dictionary (1.7). Our own short definitions of accepted Eastern Orthodox teaching and usage, drafted 2026-10-15 for the owner's and his priest's read before 1.7 ships. No Father is quoted here.

terms.definition: A long hymn of praise sung standing, from the Greek for not seated. The first akathist honors the Theotokos and is sung during Great Lent; later akathists follow its pattern of alternating stanzas and honor Christ, feasts and saints.

A solemn declaration by a council of the Church that a teaching, or a person who holds to it, stands outside the faith and communion of the Church. It guards the faithful, and the way back stays open through repentance.

Blessed bread handed out at the end of the Divine Liturgy, cut from the offered loaves but not consecrated. The name means instead of the gift. It is not Communion, and in many parishes visitors may receive it too.

A cloth signed by the bishop, usually showing Christ laid in the tomb and often with a relic sewn into it, kept on the altar table. The Divine Liturgy is served on it, and it is the sign that a parish serves with its bishop's blessing.

The chief troparion of a day, feast or saint, sung near the end of Vespers and repeated at Matins, the Hours and the Divine Liturgy. Its name comes from the dismissal, since at Vespers it comes just before the service ends.

A senior rank for a priest who is a monk. The title once named the head of a large monastery or a group of monasteries; today it is mostly a mark of honor, and bishops are often chosen from among archimandrites.

Self-headship: the standing of a local Orthodox church that chooses its own chief bishop and governs itself, while keeping one faith and full communion with the other Orthodox churches. How autocephaly is properly granted is still discussed among the churches.

The mystery of new birth, in which a person dies and rises with Christ and enters the Church. The Orthodox Church baptizes infants and adults by threefold immersion, calling on the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and Chrismation follows at once.

The chief shepherd of a local church, standing in the succession of the apostles. A bishop ordains clergy and guards the faith and unity of his flock, and every parish serves in his name. Orthodox bishops are chosen from celibate or monastic clergy.

The week that begins on Pascha, kept as one continuous day of the Resurrection. The Royal Doors stay open, the services are sung in their Paschal form, and there is no fasting, not even on Wednesday and Friday.

A rule of church order, worship or discipline set by an Ecumenical or local council or by a recognized Father. The canons serve the healing of souls, and bishops apply them with strictness or with mercy as each case requires.

A long hymn sung chiefly at Matins, built of nine odes modeled on the biblical canticles; the second ode is usually left out except in Lent. Each ode opens with an irmos and continues with troparia on the feast or saint of the day.

Someone being taught the faith and preparing for Baptism or for reception into the Church. The Divine Liturgy still prays for the catechumens just before the part of the service once kept for the baptized faithful alone.

The mystery that seals a person with the gift of the Holy Spirit, given straight after Baptism. The priest anoints the forehead, eyes, nostrils, lips, ears, chest, hands and feet with holy chrism, and some converts already baptized are received into the Church this way.

The first day of Great Lent. It follows Forgiveness Sunday, when the faithful ask one another's forgiveness at Vespers, and the Lenten fast begins as the whole Church sets out on the journey to Pascha together.

The service after the evening meal, prayed before sleep. Small Compline is read on most evenings, at home or in church; Great Compline, longer and more penitential, is served on weekdays of Great Lent and on the eves of some feasts.

The mystery of repentance, in which a person confesses sins to God in the presence of a priest, who acts as witness, gives counsel and reads the prayer of absolution. It restores a person to communion and is a regular part of Orthodox life.

An ordained minister who serves the bishop and priest at the altar, leads the litanies and reads the Gospel at the Liturgy. The Church honors St Stephen, one of the seven men chosen in Acts to serve, as archdeacon and first martyr.

Freedom from the passions, reached by God's grace through long struggle, prayer and humility. It is not coldness or indifference: the dispassionate person is free to love God and neighbor without self-seeking, and is at peace.

The Church's chief service, in which the Eucharist is offered and the faithful receive Communion. The Liturgy of St John Chrysostom is the one usually served; that of St Basil the Great is served ten times a year, and the Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts on some weekdays of Great Lent.

The feast of the Theotokos falling asleep in death, kept on 15 August after a two-week fast. The Church's tradition holds that Christ received her soul, and that after her burial she was taken up body and soul into heaven, from where she intercedes for the world.

A hymn or verse giving glory to God. The Small Doxology gives glory to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit and closes many prayers and psalms; the Great Doxology, an ancient morning hymn of praise, is sung near the end of festal Matins.

A gathering of bishops from the whole Church whose teaching the Church has received as its own faith. The Orthodox Church receives seven, from Nicaea in 325 to Nicaea in 787, which set out the faith in the Trinity, in Christ and in the holy icons.

A spiritual guide, usually a monk or nun, whom long experience of prayer and humility has made a trusted counselor of souls. The Church does not appoint elders by rank; the faithful come to recognize them over time and seek their counsel and prayers.

The prayer at the heart of the Eucharist in which the priest asks the Father to send down the Holy Spirit on the people and on the gifts of bread and wine, and to change the gifts into the Body and Blood of Christ.

A large embroidered cloth showing Christ laid in the tomb. On Great and Holy Friday it is brought out and laid in a decorated bier, the Lamentations are sung before it, and it is carried in procession around the church.

The Orthodox distinction between God's essence, which no creature can know or share, and his uncreated energies, his life and grace, in which God truly gives himself. St Gregory Palamas set it out most fully, and councils at Constantinople confirmed it in the fourteenth century.

The mystery of thanksgiving at the center of the Church's life, in which bread and wine become the true Body and Blood of Christ. Orthodox Christians prepare by prayer, fasting and confession, and receive Communion from a spoon, infants included.

Going without certain foods, usually meat, dairy, fish, wine and oil, joined to prayer and almsgiving. Most Wednesdays and Fridays are fast days, and there are four fasting seasons. The rules are kept with a spiritual father's guidance, and their strictness varies from place to place.

Latin for and the Son: a word added in the West to the Creed's article on the Holy Spirit, saying that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. The Orthodox Church keeps the Creed as the councils left it, confessing that the Spirit proceeds from the Father.

The forty days of fasting, prayer and almsgiving that prepare for Holy Week and Pascha. It begins on Clean Monday, and on weekdays the services take a penitential form, with prostrations and the Prayer of St Ephrem.

A teaching the Church has judged contrary to the faith received from the apostles, usually through a council. The word means a choice, a part picked out of the whole. Heresy is an error of doctrine, as distinct from schism, which is a break in unity.

The tradition of inner stillness and unceasing prayer, above all the Jesus Prayer, kept especially by monks. Its teachers hold that through it a person can, by grace, come to see the uncreated light of God. St Gregory Palamas defended it, and councils in the fourteenth century upheld it.
A monk who has been ordained a priest; a monk ordained a deacon is called a hierodeacon. Hieromonks serve chiefly in monasteries, and many also serve parishes.

The mystery of healing for soul and body, in which priests pray over the sick and anoint them with blessed oil, following the Letter of St James. It is given to anyone who is ill, not only the dying, and many parishes offer it to all the faithful in Holy Week.

The week from Palm Sunday to Pascha, when the Church follows Christ's last days, his Passion, death and burial. Its services are the longest and most solemn of the year, and the fast is at its strictest.

Of one essence. The word the First Council of Nicaea set in the Creed to confess that the Son is fully God with the Father, against Arius, who taught that the Son was a creature. The Church also confesses the Holy Spirit of one essence with the Father and the Son.

Four short services of psalms and prayers, the First, Third, Sixth and Ninth Hours, marking the day at about 6 and 9 in the morning, noon and 3 in the afternoon. They recall Christ's Passion and the descent of the Holy Spirit.

A distinct person or subsistence. The Church confesses one God in three hypostases, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, sharing one essence, and confesses Christ as one hypostasis, the eternal Son, in two natures, divine and human.

A holy image of Christ, the Theotokos, the saints or the feasts, painted in a traditional style. Because the Son of God became visible in the flesh, he can be depicted; the honor shown to an icon passes to the one it shows, and worship belongs to God alone.

The screen of icons between the nave and the altar. Its central Royal Doors and the deacons' doors on each side open and close during the services; facing it, Christ is on the right of the Royal Doors and the Theotokos on the left.

The eternal Son of God becoming truly human, taking flesh from the Virgin Mary by the Holy Spirit, without ceasing to be God. He is one person in two natures, so that in him human nature is healed and joined to God.
The model stanza that opens each ode of a canon. It sets the melody and meter for the troparia that follow, and it usually echoes the biblical canticle behind its ode.

A short prayer calling on the name of Jesus and asking his mercy, repeated slowly and attentively through the day. It is at the center of hesychast prayer. Many pray it with a prayer rope, a cord of knots used to count the prayers.

The area and the people under the care of a bishop or a self-governing church. In places such as the Americas, Western Europe and Australia, several Orthodox churches have parishes side by side, and the word also names each of those church bodies.

One of the twenty sections of the Psalter read at Vespers and Matins; in the full order the whole Psalter is read every week. The name comes from the Greek for sitting, since the people may sit for these readings, and it also names the short hymns sung after them.

Self-emptying: the humility of the Son of God, who without ceasing to be God took on the condition of a servant, became man and accepted death on the Cross. The word comes from the Letter of St Paul to the Philippians.

A short hymn that sums up the meaning of a feast or the life of a saint, sung at the Liturgy, at Matins after the sixth ode of the canon, and at the Hours. It descends from long sermon-hymns of the sixth century, such as those of St Romanos the Melodist.

A series of petitions led by the deacon or priest, to which the people answer each time with a short prayer for mercy or for God's grant. Litanies pray for peace, the Church, the sick, travelers, the departed and the needs of the world.

The morning service of the Church, with psalms, a canon and hymns of praise; on Sundays and feasts it includes a Gospel reading and the Great Doxology. In parishes it is served before the Divine Liturgy or, as part of a vigil, on the evening before.

A short service of prayer for the departed, asking God to give them rest with the saints. It is served after a death, on the third, ninth and fortieth days and on anniversaries, often with a dish of boiled wheat, called kollyva, blessed in their memory.

The service book in twelve volumes, one for each month beginning with September, holding the hymns for the saints and for the feasts of fixed date. Its texts join those of the Octoechos and, in season, the Triodion or Pentecostarion.

Repentance: a change of mind and heart that turns a person away from sin and back to God, renewed throughout life. The same word names a bow or prostration made in prayer, a bodily sign of that turning.

The bishop of a metropolis, originally the chief city of a province. In some churches a metropolitan leads the bishops of a region or a whole self-governing church; in the Greek tradition most diocesan bishops hold the title.

A monk or nun: someone who has left life in the world to live in prayer, obedience, chastity and poverty, usually in a monastery under an abbot or abbess. Monasticism grew in the deserts of Egypt from the late third century, and St Anthony the Great is honored as its father.

A fragrant resin or oil. It was among the gifts of the Magi and the spices the Myrrh-bearing Women brought to Christ's tomb; the holy chrism of Chrismation is called myron, and the relics or icons of some saints give off a fragrant oil, also called myrrh.

The sacred acts through which God's grace is given in the Church, called sacraments in the West. Baptism, Chrismation, the Eucharist, Confession, Holy Unction, Marriage and Holy Orders are usually named, though the Church has never strictly limited the mysteries to seven.

The feast day of the saint whose name a person bears, usually the name given at Baptism. Many Orthodox Christians keep it with more celebration than a birthday, going to church, receiving Communion and asking their patron saint's prayers.

The feast of Christ's birth in the flesh at Bethlehem, kept on 25 December after a forty-day fast; on the Old Calendar that date falls on 7 January. The Church also keeps the Nativity of the Theotokos on 8 September and of St John the Baptist on 24 June.

The Revised Julian calendar, which keeps the fixed feasts on the civil dates, so that Nativity falls on 25 December. Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch, Greece, Romania and Bulgaria are among the churches that follow it; like the Old Calendar churches, nearly all of them keep Pascha by the Julian reckoning.

The spiritual intellect, the highest faculty of the soul, by which a person can know God directly in prayer rather than by reasoning alone. The Fathers teach that the fallen nous is scattered and darkened, and that prayer and repentance gather and purify it.

The service book of the eight tones, the sets of melodies in which Orthodox hymns are sung. Each week has its own tone, starting again every eight weeks, and the book gives the resurrection hymns and daily hymns for each. Tradition links it with St John of Damascus.

One of the nine songs from Scripture, such as those of Moses, Hannah and the Theotokos, on which the canon at Matins is built; also each of the nine parts of a canon. Each ode of a canon opens with an irmos.

The Julian calendar, now thirteen days behind the civil calendar, so that its 25 December falls on the civil 7 January. The churches of Jerusalem, Russia, Serbia and Georgia and the monasteries of Mount Athos follow it. Nearly all Orthodox keep Pascha on the same day, whichever calendar they follow.

Essence or being: what a thing is, as distinct from who someone is. The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are three hypostases who share one essence wholly, and God's essence remains beyond all knowing.

All-holy: a title often given to the Theotokos, especially among Greek Orthodox Christians, honoring her as the holiest of all creatures. It also names churches dedicated to her, and the small icon of her that a bishop wears on his chest.

The feast of Christ's Resurrection, the Feast of Feasts, whose name comes from the Hebrew for Passover. Its date, a Sunday in spring, is reckoned by the Julian calendar, so it often falls later than the Western Easter, and its celebration begins at midnight with a joyful procession.

Disordered desires and habits, such as gluttony, lust, greed, anger, despondency, vainglory and pride, that grip the soul and turn its God-given powers away from their purpose. They are healed by God's grace through repentance, prayer, fasting and the mysteries.

The chief bishop of certain self-governing churches, among them Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem, Moscow, Serbia, Romania, Bulgaria and Georgia. A patriarch governs with his synod of bishops; the Patriarch of Constantinople, called the Ecumenical Patriarch, holds the first place of honor among them.

The feast of the Holy Spirit's descent on the apostles, fifty days after Pascha, often called the birthday of the Church. It is also kept as the feast of the Holy Trinity, and at its Vespers the faithful kneel for the first time since Pascha.
The service book and season from Pascha to the Sunday of All Saints, a week after Pentecost. It holds the hymns of Pascha, the Ascension and Pentecost, and of the Sundays between them.

A collection of writings on watchfulness and prayer of the heart, from Fathers of the fourth to the fifteenth centuries, gathered by St Nikodemos the Hagiorite and St Makarios of Corinth and published at Venice in 1782. St Paisius Velichkovsky's Slavonic translation spread it through Russia.

The prayers a person keeps each day, usually morning and evening prayers from the prayer book, set with the help of a spiritual father. A rule is meant to be kept faithfully and with attention, and a short rule kept steadily is better than a long one abandoned.

Spiritual delusion: a state of pride in which a person takes imaginings, or the deceptions of the evil one, for grace and holiness. Humility, obedience to a spiritual father and caution toward visions guard against it.

An ordained presbyter who serves the mysteries and cares for a parish on behalf of the bishop. A priest may marry before ordination but not after; many parish priests are married, while a priest who is a monk is called a hieromonk.
A psalm verse, with one or more further verses, sung before a reading from Scripture, chiefly before the Epistle at the Divine Liturgy, and at every Vespers. The name means that which is set before.

The leavened bread baked for the Divine Liturgy, often by the faithful, and stamped with a seal whose letters mean Jesus Christ conquers. The priest cuts the Lamb from it for consecration, and the rest is shared out as antidoron.

A man tonsured and blessed by the bishop to read the Epistle, the psalms and other texts in the services. It is the first of the minor orders, below subdeacon, and in many parishes others also read with a blessing.

The bodies or bones of the saints, and things they used, honored because the grace that sanctified the saints still rests on them. Relics are placed in the altar when a church is consecrated, are often sewn into the antimension, and God has worked many healings through them.

A holy one: someone in whom God's grace has shone, who now lives with Christ and prays for the world. The Church does not make saints but recognizes them, in a service of glorification, and honors them with a feast day, an icon and hymns.

The monastic habit, and the degree of monastic life it marks. The Great Schema is the highest degree, with the strictest rule of prayer; in some traditions it is given only after long years or near death, in others at the monk's main tonsure.

A break in the unity and communion of the Church, distinguished from heresy, which is an error of doctrine. The best known is the estrangement between Rome and the Orthodox East, conventionally dated to 1054, which grew over centuries.

The priest who guides a person's spiritual life over time, usually by hearing his or her confession, and helps set a prayer rule and the measure of fasting. Experienced monks and nuns who are not ordained may also guide others, as spiritual fathers and mothers.
One of the minor orders, above reader and below deacon. A subdeacon helps in the altar, cares for the vestments and sacred vessels, and assists the bishop at his services, for example by vesting him.
A collection of short lives of the saints and accounts of the feasts, arranged by day of the year. The day's entry is traditionally read at Matins after the sixth ode of the canon.

The feast of Christ's baptism in the Jordan, kept on 6 January, when the Holy Trinity was revealed: the Father's voice, the Son in the water and the Spirit as a dove. The Church blesses water on this day, and the faithful take it home.

Deification: the goal of the Christian life, union with God by grace. Through God's uncreated energies, never his essence, a person comes to share in God's own life while remaining a creature. It begins in this life through the Church's mysteries, prayer and keeping the commandments.

A hymn to the Theotokos that closes a group of hymns, usually following the Small Doxology. Almost every set of troparia, stichera and canon odes ends with one, so that she is honored throughout the services.

God-bearer: the Church's title for the Virgin Mary, confirmed by the Third Ecumenical Council at Ephesus in 431, because the one she bore is God the Son made man. The Church honors her as ever-virgin and above all the saints, and asks her prayers.

The feast, on 6 August, of Christ shining with divine light on Mount Tabor before Peter, James and John, with Moses and Elijah beside him. The Church sees that light as the uncreated light of God, and grapes and other fruit are blessed on the day.

The one God in three persons, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, one in essence and equal in glory. The Father is the source: the Son is eternally begotten of him and the Spirit eternally proceeds from him. The Church worships one God, not three.

The service book and season of the ten weeks before Pascha, from the Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee through Great Lent and Holy Week. Its name comes from the canons of three odes sung on Lenten weekdays.

The thrice-holy hymn, calling God holy, mighty and immortal and asking his mercy, sung at the Divine Liturgy and said at the start of daily prayers. The Trisagion prayers built around it open most services, and a short Trisagion service is also prayed for the departed.

A short hymn, one stanza long, that expresses the meaning of a feast or the life of a saint. The word is used broadly for many stanzas in the services, and most often for the apolytikion, the chief hymn of the day.

The chief feasts of the year, ranked below Pascha alone: the Nativity of the Theotokos, the Exaltation of the Cross, the Entry of the Theotokos, the Nativity of Christ, Theophany, the Meeting of the Lord, the Annunciation, Palm Sunday, the Ascension, Pentecost, the Transfiguration and the Dormition.

The book of rules that sets the order of the services through the year: which hymns and readings are used, how feasts that fall on the same day are combined, and how the fasts are kept. Parishes follow it with local adaptations.

The evening service that begins the liturgical day, since the Church counts each day from sunset. It includes the evening psalm of creation, the lamp-lighting psalms with their hymns, an ancient hymn to Christ as the joyful light, and the Song of Simeon.

A long service on the eve of a Sunday or feast that joins Vespers, Matins and the First Hour. In monasteries, especially on Mount Athos, it can last through the night; in most parishes it is shortened to a few hours.

Sober attention to the heart: guarding the mind against tempting thoughts as they first appear, so that they are turned away before they take hold. The Fathers join it to the Jesus Prayer, and the Philokalia gathers their teaching on it.

Dry eating: the strict form of fasting, with no meat, fish, dairy, eggs, oil or wine, only bread, vegetables, fruit, nuts and pulses, kept on many weekdays of Great Lent and Holy Week. How strictly it is kept varies between churches and with a spiritual father's guidance.
